title: Correlation and least-squares regression
subtitle: Do two quantities move together, and can one predict the other? Fit the line that makes the smallest total squared miss.

sections.title: Scatter plots and correlation
sections.body:
Do taller people weigh more? Do hotter days sell more ice cream? To find out you plot pairs (x, y) and look for a pattern. The correlation coefficient r = Sxy/√(Sxx·Syy) puts a number on it, between −1 and 1: +1 is a perfect rising line, −1 a perfect falling one, and 0 means no linear relation.

For the default data r = 0.9; a falling line gives -1. Two warnings you must remember: correlation is not causation, and r ignores curved patterns. So r = −0.95 means a strong falling linear relationship.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: r is not a percentage change.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Sign gives direction, size gives strength.

keynotes: The correlation coefficient r = Sxy/√(Sxx·Syy) lies in [−1, 1]: +1 is a perfect rising line, −1 a perfect falling one, and 0 means no linear relation.
For the default data r = 0.9; a falling line gives −1.
Correlation is not causation, and r ignores curved patterns.

sections.title: The least-squares line
sections.body:
Many lines pass near a cloud of points, so which is best? The one with the smallest total squared miss. Fit ŷ = a + bx by minimising Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². The solution is b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ȳ − b·x̄, so the line always passes through (x̄, ȳ). The residuals are the vertical gaps; squaring them punishes big misses. In the figure, the line pivots on the mean point.

Try the data (1,2) (2,3) (3,5) (4,4) (5,6): x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4. Sxy = 9, Sxx = 10. Slope = 9/10 = 0.9, intercept = 4 − 0.9·3 = 1.3. The least-squares line always passes through the point of means.

questions.prompt: The least-squares line always passes through…

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It fits the cloud, not one point.

figures.caption: Figure 4.2.1 — least squares
figures.note: The line pivots on the mean point; gaps are the residuals.

problems.prompt: Predict y at x = 6 using the fitted line.
problems.answer: ŷ = 1.3 + 0.9·6 = 6.7 (x = 6 is just outside the data — mild extrapolation).

keynotes: Least squares fits ŷ = a + bx by minimising Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)², with b = Sxy/Sxx and a = ȳ − b·x̄.
The line always passes through (x̄, ȳ).
For the data (1,2) (2,3) (3,5) (4,4) (5,6) the slope is 0.9 and the intercept 1.3.

sections.title: How good is the fit? R²
sections.body: How good is the line, as you can judge? R² = 1 − SSres/SStot is the fraction of the variation in y explained by x; for simple regression R² = r². This fit has R² = 0.81, which means 81 % explained. So r = 0.9 gives R² = 0.81. But beware: a high R² does not prove the model is right. Always look at the residual plot for curves or fan shapes.

sections.title: Pitfalls
sections.body:
Regression is powerful and easy to abuse. Here are the four traps you should learn to spot.

  • Extrapolation beyond the data range is unreliable.
  • Outliers with large leverage can tilt the line.
  • Non-linear patterns: transform (log y) or use a curve.
  • Confounders: ice-cream sales and drownings correlate because of summer.

The best explanation for shark attacks and ice-cream sales rising together? A third factor, hot weather, drives both.

questions.prompt: Shark attacks and ice-cream sales correlate. Best explanation?

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: There is a real common cause.

keynotes: Extrapolation beyond the data range is unreliable.
Outliers with large leverage can tilt the line; non-linear patterns need a transform (log y) or a curve.
Confounders can fake a relationship: ice-cream sales and drownings correlate because of summer.

sections.title: More than one predictor
sections.body: One predictor is rarely enough. Multiple regression fits ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … by the same least-squares idea, which means you solve the normal equations XᵀXb = Xᵀy (the Gaussian elimination of Numerical Methods). Gradient descent finds the same minimum iteratively, which is how machine-learning models are trained. Solving the normal equations is a linear algebra problem.

keynotes: Multiple regression fits ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … by least squares.

sections.title: Rank correlation
sections.body:
What if your data are ranks, like judges scoring a contest, not measurements? Spearman’s ρ applies the correlation formula to the ranks: ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)), d = rank difference. It detects any monotone relationship and resists outliers.

Two judges ranking five entries with Σd² = 4 give ρ = 1 − 24/120 = 0.8. And if Σd² = 0 the judges agree perfectly, so ρ = 1.
